Photograph: ICAC View image in fullscreen Dallas McInerney has told the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption that Catholic Schools NSW funding wasn’t misused. Photograph: ICAC Independent Commission Against Corruption Teachers demand more scrutiny of Catholic school funding amid allegations of ‘sham arrangement’ with NSW Liberal group Independent Education Union ‘deeply concerned … public funding for Catholic schools may have been wrongfully spent on Liberal party matters’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Penry Buckley Fri 14 Aug 2026 03.41 EDT First published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 03.29 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The union for independent school teachers in New South Wales has demanded greater scrutiny of Catholic schools as the chief executive of their governing body told a corruption inquiry payments to a lobbying firm were not a “sham arrangement” to fund Liberal party factional work. Dallas McInerney insisted to the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Friday that Catholic Schools NSW funding wasn’t misused. Icac is investigating whether McInerney arranged and approved illegal donations from the governing body for 600 Catholic schools to support alleged branch stacking efforts of the Christian factional group the Reformers. The group wanted more conservative policies on issues such as abortion, euthanasia and same-sex marriage. The inquiry has heard that Catholic Schools NSW paid Beckington, a lobbying company run by Reformers Christian Ellis and Jeremy Greenwood, $130,900 through invoices for consulting services between August 2019 and August 2021. Alleged victim of Alan Jones made broadcaster soft-boiled eggs with soldiers and ironed his underpants, court told Read more Greenwood’s company, JPG Advisory, was paid $135,000 between December 2021 and December 2023. The commission has heard that Reformers Robert Assaf and Dylan Whitelaw spent work hours on factional efforts while employed at Catholic Schools NSW. On Friday, the Independent Education Union’s NSW branch, which had previously declined to comment while the inquiry was under way, said it was “deeply concerned by … [allegations] that public funding for Catholic schools may have been wrongfully spent on Liberal party matters”. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The IEU NSW/ACT branch secretary, Carol Matthews, said close scrutiny of public funding “was not applied to organisations such as Catholic Schools NSW that receive funding on behalf of Catholic diocesan schools”. “Regardless of the findings of Icac in this matter, there should be greater scrutiny of bodies such as Catholic Schools NSW, which receive public funding on behalf of non-government schools,” Matthews said in a statement. About 80% of the funding distributed by Catholic Schools NSW comes from the state and federal governments. Government funding totalled about $3.8bn in 2024. The NSW premier, Chris Minns, has ruled out an independent audit of the schools governing body while Icac’s inquiry is under way. McInerney stood aside from his role as CEO before the Icac hearings began “to allow the work of Catholic Schools NSW to continue its important mission”, he said in a statement previously. Catholic Schools NSW has previously said it “does not intend … to provide responses to questions that supersede the eight-week inquiry and legal process that is under way”. McInerney on Friday was asked about messages in February 2021 between Assaf and fellow Reformer Jean-Claude Perrottet, the younger brother of former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet, who is not accused of wrongdoing. Assaf and Jean-Claude were not directly employed by Beckington. Jean-Claude Perrottet wrote to Assaf: “Ellis and I caught up with Dallas in Bowral to discuss money, had a long convo.” The counsel assisting Juliet Curtin asked if the reason for Assaf and Jean-Claude’s interest was “because they knew that the arrangement in place was that you would pay Beckington money pursuant to a sham arrangement” – under which the money would come to them. “No,” McInerney said on Friday. He said he could not recall the Bowral meeting. McInerney rejected evidence previously given by Assaf to the inquiry that Greenwood and McInerney met this year to discuss their summons. The inquiry has previously heard that Jean-Claude Perrottet received money from Beckington. When the Catholic Schools NSW contract moved in 2021 from Beckington to JPG Advisory, Assaf and Jean-Claude allegedly each received a “kickback”, in Jean-Claude’s case, 50% of the monthly retainer, after he secured the contract with McInerney. On Friday, McInerney repeatedly described Jean-Claude Perrottet as his “conduit” to Greenwood, who ran JPG. Dylan Whitelaw, who worked at Beckington after being employed by McInerney at Catholic Schools NSW, has previously given evidence there was an arrangement under which payments from the schools’ governing body to Beckington were used to fund Reformers’ activities. McInerney repeatedly denied this. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion McInerney was asked on Friday why Whitelaw, then only 21, was involved in negotiating an increase in Beckington’s retainer in 2021, and why McInerney cited Whitelaw’s departure from the company as a reason to end the contract with Beckington. “I’m not confident they’ll have the in-house expertise to support our needs in the way DW [Dylan Whitelaw] has been,” McInerney wrote to a colleague. On Friday, McInerney, who described Whitelaw as a “junior” at Beckington who carried out an “account manager” role and was responsible for “administrative interplay”, said his language had been consistent. “Your in-house expertise as an account manager is … knowing the client, the rhythms, the relationships, how they service,” he said. The inquiry has previously heard that McInerney came to know Whitelaw through the Mittagoing Liberal branch after first meeting his parents. He employed Whitelaw at Catholic Schools NSW in 2019 after he graduated high school. On Thursday, McInerney said correspondence leading up to the Beckington contract in which he told Ellis to get an ABN and a mailbox was “traditional due diligence”. He denied he was attempting to provide “a veneer of legitimacy” to the contract. On Friday, the inquiry – and McInerney – learned that the ABN provided by Ellis in fact belonged to Ellis’s sister. After Curtin suggested it showed due diligence “wasn’t particularly effective”, McInerney said: “I will add the point [that] I thought it was, but I’m happy to be enlightened”. The inquiry heard Beckington later wrote Catholic Schools NSW’s name incorrectly on invoices. After Curtin suggested evidence of written work by Beckington was “de minimis”, apart from calendar entries for monthly meetings, McInerney insisted Beckington did consult for Catholic Schools NSW. Asked if Beckington’s input was “only ever given orally”, McInerney said that Beckington had contributed to two “forward plans for public affairs and engagement in 2019” which involved “exhaustive planning sessions”. The commission heard McInerney provided the two documents but there was no written evidence of Beckington being involved in the drafting process. McInerney was expected to appear again before Icac next week. https://www.dw.com/en/pakistan-top-court.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Izu9 Former cricketer Imran Khan served as prime minister from 2018 to 2022 [File photo: March 2023] Image: Akhtar Soomro/REUTERS Advertisement Pakistan 's Supreme Court on Tuesday ordered that jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan be moved to hospital for medical checks after his lawyers filed a petition citing poor health . The top court said the 73-year-old would be transferred to Shifa International hospital in the capital, Islamabad, within two days. The cricketer-turned-politician was jailed in 2023 after being convicted on a string of charges that he claims were politically motivated. Khan's party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), and his family have repeatedly raised fears about his health in prison. His lawyers have also stated that he has lost most of the vision in his right eye. Khan ally welcomes decision Tuesday's order came after a medical team examined Khan at Rawalpnidi's Adiala jail last week, where it recorded high blood pressure, palpitations and anxiety. "It's a very welcome order and we wish it had happened sooner so his eye and general health would not have deteriorated this much," Sayed Zulfikar Bukhari, a close Khan aide, said in a statement. "He should remain in hospital until all doctors are satisfied," he added. Khan's spokesperson said he was expected to remain in hospital until September 16. Why is Khan in jail? Khan was Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022 . Following his ouster in a no-confidence vote, he was convicted on a number of charges including allegations of an unlawful marriage and corruption . He was sentenced late last year , along with his wife, to 17 years in prison for graft. Both deny wrongdoing. PTI still enjoys significant support across key provinces in Pakistan, and Khan himself remains a popular figure. His arrest in early 2023 triggered nationwide protests that resulted in hundreds of people being arrested. Earlier this year, cricket greats from around the world appealed to the Pakistani government for Khan to receive proper medical treatment in prison, calling in a letter for "decency and justice." Photograph: Judith Jockel/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Mohammed Shirwa, an Uber driver from Rotterdam, claims Uber’s pay-setting mechanism preys on weakness. Photograph: Judith Jockel/The Guardian Uber Uber drivers launch European class action over ‘soulless’ and ‘scary’ AI algorithm Landmark lawsuit claims tech company’s pay-setting system has breached privacy laws and pushed down earnings Robert Booth UK technology editor Wed 2 Sep 2026 11.37 EDT Last modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 11.50 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Uber drivers have launched a landmark legal action against the ride-hailing company claiming they live in “constant fear” of a “soulless” algorithm it uses to set pay and allocate jobs. Drivers from the UK, the Netherlands and other countries have joined the compensation claim that could run into billions of dollars. It alleges an AI-powered pay-setting system breaches data protection laws and pushes down their earnings. The claim has been filed at Amsterdam’s district court, where the $150bn (£111bn) San Francisco tech company has its European HQ. It is the first collective legal move of its kind, according to the European Trade Union Confederation. The case centres on an opaque “black box” algorithm fed on information about drivers, which sets a personalised rate for each ride. Drivers fear it pushes down fares to the minimum they are willing to accept. Drivers have told the Guardian the algorithm has offered the same job to different people at different pay rates and offers them less for a return journey after a long trip because it calculates they will not want to come home empty. “It is like someone watching you all the time and knowing about your weakness – the boss is the algorithm,” said Mohammed Shirwa, a 41-year-old Uber driver in Rotterdam. “All the time the algorithm is learning about you and what you are willing to accept. So the prices go low but you are stuck. It knows you need the job.” View image in fullscreen Kola Oba, from Tottenham in north London, claims Uber exploits information it collects about him to push down fares. Kola Oba, who calls the algorithm “soulless”, was taking a break in Tottenham, north London, with another driver when they were offered the same job. The other driver was offered £27 and Oba was offered £23. The pair suspected it was because Oba, 48, had taken several cheap jobs and the AI assumed he would accept a lower price. Uber has previously said such discrepancies were down to other features of its system including GPS, surge pricing, promotions and testing. “It’s scary – they have all my information and they are using it against my own wellbeing,” Oba said. “It defines how much I earn, how long I have to work, my time with my family, my resting time.” AI models take an increasing role in assigning work to humans by using their rapidly increasing power to learn about a business’s needs and staff behaviour and then acting as a “synthetic manager”. The Dutch data protection authority fined ⁠Uber €825m (£708m) last month for deactivating driver ⁠accounts through automated systems without ​adequate notice. Uber said it would appeal. The company is also planning to roll out driverless cars in European cities from London to Zagreb, initially with human supervisions. The legal case is being led by the Worker Info Exchange, a campaign group whose founder, James Farrar, secured a UK supreme court ruling that Uber drivers should have worker rights. Relating to about 241,000 drivers across the EU and the UK, the claim alleges that Uber has unlawfully used automated decision-making, including profiling, in dynamically setting pay and allocating work. The lawsuit, which also claims the company unlawfully used driver data to train its AI models, is seeking damages for affected drivers and an injunction to halt the conduct which it claims breaches GDPR data regulations. The drivers claim Uber has operated dynamic pay-setting in the UK since 2023, pushing down their annual incomes by about £5,000. The system was introduced in the Netherlands this year. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Uber’s chief executive, Dara Khosrowshahi, said in 2023 : “I think that what we can do better is targeting of different trips to different drivers based on their preferences or based on behavioural patterns that they’re showing us.” View image in fullscreen Uber, which has its headquarters in San Francisco, said it categorically rejected the allegations. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images Uber said it did not adjust the price offered for a trip based on an individual driver’s behaviour and that a history of accepting or rejecting trips was not used to personalise pay offers. Instead, it said, dynamic pricing allowed it to increase pay on less attractive trips, boosting a driver’s earning potential. “While we haven’t seen the claim yet, we categorically reject the allegations,” an Uber spokesperson said. “The Uber app uses real-time information about the trip such as journey, duration and destination to calculate fares. “Drivers see their earnings and where a trip is going before they decide whether to accept it. The vast majority of total fares continue to go where they belong: into drivers’ pockets, and the percentage that Uber keeps from fares has remained relatively flat .” A 2025 study by academics at the University of Oxford, which Uber said relied on incomplete and selective data, found there had been substantial cuts in driver earnings after the “dynamic” algorithm was introduced. Farrar said: “It’s bad enough that Uber’s dynamic pay algorithms have squeezed driver pay for years now but the intrusive and underhanded way in which Uber uses its technology to monitor and influence drivers’ behaviour is an affront to their dignity as workers and as human beings.” Anton Ekker, a Dutch lawyer leading the case, said: “A computer algorithm should not independently make decisions that strip individuals of their livelihood. Like so many other online platforms, it should be held accountable for the large-scale exploitation of vulnerabilities of European citizens.” Explore more on these topics Uber AI (artificial intelligence) Transport Gig economy Europe Netherlands GDPR news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story ‘Leicester Square, please guv’: Self-driving taxis cleared for London streets ‘later this summer’ Uber to buy Germany’s Delivery Hero in $14.8bn global deal Dynamic pay on platforms such as Uber should be banned, says TUC Uber driver Michael was assaulted by passengers.
